11.t: Working with data: yeast and sugar
q: Calculate the mean rate of CO₂ production with 10% glucose between 10 and 30 minutes. Give the units.
(13.2 − 3.4) / 20 = 0.49 cm³ min⁻¹. One mark for the working, one for the value with units.
Explain why CO₂ production with 2% glucose levels off after 20 minutes.
The glucose is being used up, so the substrate becomes limiting. With no sugar left to ferment, no more CO₂ is made (about 5 cm³ in total).
A student concludes: "more glucose always means faster respiration". Evaluate this claim.

Supported from 2% to 10%: CO₂ is faster and keeps rising. Not supported at 40%: the slowest of all. A very concentrated solution draws water out of the yeast cells by osmosis, slowing their enzymes. Only three concentrations were tested, so the best one is not known.
Suggest why all three curves are slow to rise in the first 5 minutes.
The yeast needs time to warm up and take up glucose; some CO₂ dissolves in the water before gas collects; the air in the flask must be used first (aerobic respiration).
Yeast can also respire aerobically. Outline how you could show that some of the CO₂ came from anaerobic respiration.
Test the liquid for ethanol (smell, or acidified dichromate turning green). Only anaerobic respiration makes ethanol. Or cover the liquid with oil so no oxygen can enter and show CO₂ is still made.

20.t: Working with data: blocking the Krebs cycle
q: Describe the changes in succinate and fumarate between 10 and 20 minutes. Use figures.
Succinate rises 7-fold (10 to 70 au) while fumarate falls from 10 to 1 au.
Deduce which reaction malonate blocks. Explain your answer.
Succinate to fumarate (succinate dehydrogenase). The substrate builds up before the block and the product disappears after it.
Explain why oxygen uptake falls, although oxygen is not used in the Krebs cycle.

With the cycle stopped, fewer reduced NAD and FAD are made, so fewer electrons reach the electron transport chain. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, so less is used. (Succinate dehydrogenase also passes electrons straight into the chain.)
After extra succinate was added, oxygen uptake partly recovered. Deduce the type of inhibitor malonate is.
Competitive: malonate is similar in shape to succinate and binds the active site. A higher substrate concentration outcompetes it, so activity partly returns.
Predict the effect of malonate on the rate of ATP production. Explain.
It falls: fewer electrons flow, so fewer protons are pumped, the proton gradient is smaller and less ATP is made by ATP synthase (chemiosmosis).

27.t: Working with data: poisons and brown fat
q: Explain why cyanide stops both oxygen use and ATP production.
Cyanide blocks the last carrier of the electron transport chain, so electrons cannot pass to oxygen. No electron flow means no proton pumping, no gradient and no ATP.
Oligomycin blocks only ATP synthase, yet oxygen use falls by 75%. Explain why.

Protons cannot flow back through ATP synthase, so the proton gradient builds up. Pumping against this steep gradient becomes too hard, so electron flow slows and less oxygen is reduced. Electron flow and ATP synthesis are coupled.
Compare the effects of DNP and oligomycin. Explain the difference in oxygen use.
Both stop almost all ATP production. Oligomycin lowers oxygen use; DNP raises it (160%). DNP lets protons leak back, so the gradient never builds and the chain runs as fast as it can.
Use the data to explain how brown fat keeps a newborn baby warm.
UCP1 lets protons leak back without ATP synthase, so the energy of the gradient is released as heat (200% of the control) instead of being stored in ATP.
DNP was once sold as a slimming pill. Suggest why it caused weight loss and why it was dangerous.
To make enough ATP, much more fat and sugar is respired, so mass falls. But the extra heat can cause fatal overheating, and cells run short of ATP.
